newsitem.title: USA: Clinton accuser Hale to stand trial.
newsitem.headline: Clinton accuser Hale to stand trial.

text.p: President Clinton's accuser in the Whitewater affair, former Arkansas businessman David Hale, was ordered Monday to stand trial for filing false statements about an insurance company he owned.
Hale has pleaded not guilty but prosecutor Larry Jegley charged that he deliberately misled Arkansas regulators about the financial health of his burial insurance company, which eventually collapsed.

State Circuit Judge David Bogard refused defence motions to dismiss the charge against Hale and set trial for Sept. 22. But he also agreed to hold a Sept. 16 hearing on claims by Hale that his plea bargain with Whitewater prosecutors precluded his prosecution on state charges.
"This case doesn't have beans to do with what the Whitewater prosecutors were doing," Jegley told reporters.
Defence attorney David Bowden said Whitewater prosecutors had refused to support his argument for immunity. "We've agreed to disagree," Bowden said.

Dressed in prison denim and sneakers, Hale, 56, was brought to the Little Rock courtroom from a federal prison in Texarkana, Texas, where he is serving a 28-month sentence for his conviction in the Whitewater case. He faces up to eight years in prison if convicted in the upcoming state trial.

He came to national attention in 1994 when he told investigators that President Clinton had pressured him to make an illegal loan to Susan McDougal, one of Clinton's partners in an Arkansas real estate project called Whitewater.

Hale owned a federally insured small business lending company, Capital Management Services. It was seized in 1992 by the federal government, which found that a great majority of the company's loans were in default and had been illegally diverted to projects in which Hale had controlling interest.

Hale pleaded guilty in March, 1994 to fraud and agreed to cooperate with the Whitewater special prosecutor. In 1996 he testified for the government in the trial of McDougal and her former husband, James McDougal, another Whitewater investor. Both were convicted of fraud and conspiracy and are in prison.
Clinton testified for the defence, insisting he had no knowledge of the loan Hale made to Susan McDougal.
Prosecutors said a portion of the loan was improperly diverted to the Whitewater project in which the McDougals and Clinton and his wife had an interest.
